newsitem.title: UK: Campaigners urge US, UK to press Bahrain on rights.
newsitem.headline: Campaigners urge US, UK to press Bahrain on rights.

text.p: Human rights campaigners on Monday urged the United States and British governments to put more pressure on the authorities in Bahrain to release political prisoners and end abuses such as the torture of detainees.
On the day Bahrain marked its silver jubilee, British human rights campaigner Lord Avebury said he had been told of demonstrations, a student boycott and reports of explosions in the Gulf state.

Listing human rights abuses such as the forced exile of dissidents, the dismissal of government critics from their jobs and unfair trials, the campaigners called on Bahrain's ruling family to enter into a dialogue with pro-democracy activists.
Amnesty International official Hania Mufti issued an appeal to the British, U.S. and other governments "to exert more pressure to try and alleviate the suffering of the people of Bahrain".
She was speaking at a London news conference called by the British Parliamentary Human Rights Group, Amnesty, Human Rights Watch-Middle East and the Arab Organisation for Human Rights.
Amnesty and Human Rights Watch officials put the number detained in Bahrain at between 1,000 and 1,500.

Avebury, chairman of the Parliamentary Human Rights Group, said: "Considering the close relationship that exists between Britain and the United States on the one hand and Bahrain on the other, we could be more influential than we have been."
Avebury said that for the majority of Bahrain's population who are Shi'ite Moslems, the 25th anniversary of Bahrain's independence was "a reminder of their oppression" by the ruling Sunni Moslems.

He said that on Sunday, acording to local people, lights had been turned out in residential areas of Bahrain in an anti-government protest, students had boycotted classes, tyres had been burned in the streets and two explosions had been heard, while one civilian had been injured.
Bahrain, a British protectorate from 1861 to 1971, has seen sporadic internal unrest over the last two years in which about 27 people have died.
Dissident Shi'ites want the country's rulers to make economic and political reforms including restoring a parliament dissolved in 1975 and the lifting of a ban on political parties.
Avebury welcomed decisions by the Bahrain authorities to release a number of prisoners and to allow the International Committee of the Red Cross access to people in detention.

But he said 18 people, including three boys aged between eight and 15, had been arrested this month and a pattern was emerging whereby people were detained for short periods and abused before being freed, to avoid Red Cross scrutiny.
He also criticised the British head of the Bahrain security service, Ian Henderson, who is believed to be about to retire to Britain.

"Torture in Bahrain is unfortunately rather common and it is a matter of shame and regret that the man in charge of the security apparatus and so ultimately responsible for these atrocities is a Briton, Mr Ian Henderson," Avebury said.
"I hope the law will allow him to be sued in the (British) civil courts by some of his victims or their bereaved families."
